q-47079.name: Question 1
q-47079.worked_solution:
We can evaluate this limit using direct substitution, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to 3}{2}^{(-2x+4)} & ={2}^{(-2(3)+4)} \\  & ={2}^{(-2)} \\  & =\frac{1}{{2}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{1}{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

q-339071.name: Question 2
q-339071.worked_solution:
We can evaluate this limit using direct substitution, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to 0}\frac{{e}^{x}+2}{{2}^{x}+3} & =\frac{{lim}_{x\to 0}({e}^{x}+2)}{{lim}_{x\to 0}({2}^{x}+3)} \\  & =\frac{{e}^{0}+2}{{2}^{0}+3} \\  & =\frac{1+2}{1+3} \\  & =\frac{3}{4}\end{aligned}
$$

q-99515.name: Question 5
q-99515.worked_solution:
We can use the algebra of limits to rewrite the given limit, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to -\infty }\frac{7{e}^{3x-8}}{3} & ={lim}_{x\to -\infty }(\frac{7}{3}\cdot {e}^{3x}\cdot {e}^{-8}) \\  & =\frac{7{e}^{-8}}{3}\cdot {lim}_{x\to -\infty }{e}^{3x}\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we recall the graph of $y={e}^{3x}.$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/linear/14258364/assets/df39137953015b819f3143e823f042ac759a8dfb356821ce6f623b40924b0b0c.png)

From the graph, we see that the function decreases to zero as $x$ decreases. Therefore, 

$$
{lim}_{x\to -\infty }{e}^{3x}=0.
$$

We conclude that

$$
\frac{7{e}^{-8}}{3}\cdot {lim}_{x\to -\infty }{e}^{3x}=\frac{7{e}^{-8}}{3}\cdot 0=0.
$$
